extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent applicants and practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examination of patentability under 35 U.S.C. §§ 101, 102, 103, and 112, including subject-matter eligibility, utility, novelty, non-obviousness, and specification/claim requirements. Used by examiners to formulate rejections and by applicants to respond or amend claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four Categories of Statutory Subject Matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory subject matter comprises processes, machines, manufactures, and compositions of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must fall within one of these categories to be statutory subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101. Examiners assess whether the claimed invention is a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial Exceptions (Step 2A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial exceptions include abstract ideas; laws of nature and natural phenomena; and products of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the Step 2A analysis, determine whether the claim recites or is directed to a judicial exception. If so, proceed to prong two (integration into a practical application).

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly Different Characteristics Test
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether claims possess characteristics that are 'markedly different' from naturally occurring items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For claims involving natural products, examine whether the claimed subject matter exhibits markedly different characteristics (structure, function, or other properties) relative to the natural product. If markedly different, the claim may be patent eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration into Practical Application (Step 2A Prong Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must show integration of judicial exceptions into a practical, real-world application rather than mere recitation of the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether additional claim limitations integrate the exception into a practical application (e.g., by applying the exception in a specific technological environment or improving a technological process). Mere field-of-use or generic computer implementation is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significantly More Analysis (Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether claims amount to 'significantly more' than the judicial exception by adding inventive concepts or improvements to technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Step 2B, look for limitations that provide an inventive concept beyond the exception—examples include improvements to computer functionality or other technological improvements. If the claim elements do no more than well-understood, routine, conventional activity, eligibility is lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility Requirement (35 U.S.C. § 101)
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must possess specific, substantial, and credible utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must provide an adequate showing of utility; special considerations and evidentiary standards apply for therapeutic or pharmacological utilities (e.g., credible evidence of utility for a claimed pharmaceutical use). Vague or speculative utilities are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty / Anticipation — Post-AIA Standards (35 U.S.C. § 102)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention is anticipated if patented, described in a printed publication, or otherwise publicly available before the effective filing date, or by certain earlier-filed U.S. patent documents naming another inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine prior art disclosures to determine whether a single reference discloses every claim limitation. Consider effective filing dates, priority claims, and whether the reference is enabling. Anticipation requires a clear, enabling disclosure of the claimed subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace Period Exceptions (Novelty)
rubrics_metrics.description: One-year grace period applies for inventor-originated disclosures and prior public disclosures by the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the AIA, certain disclosures made by the inventor (or derived from the inventor) within one year before the effective filing date may not count as prior art. Properly analyze whether a disclosure qualifies for the grace period and whether evidence supports inventor origination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty / Anticipation — Pre-AIA Standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-AIA anticipation includes knowledge or use by others in the country, public use or sale in the country, foreign patents or publications, and prior U.S. applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For applications with pre-AIA effective dates, apply the statutory pre-AIA definitions of prior art, including on-sale and public-use bars, and relevant foreign documents and prior applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-Obviousness — Prima Facie Obviousness (35 U.S.C. § 103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie case of obviousness requires: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the prior art and the claimed invention; (3) the level of ordinary skill in the art; (4) a motivation to combine references; and (5) a reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Graham framework to evaluate obviousness. The examiner must articulate how the references, knowledge, and reasoning lead to a conclusion of obviousness, addressing each Graham factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner Reliance Sources for Obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may rely on implicit disclosures in references, scientific theory and common knowledge, art-recognized equivalence and suitability, and homologs and structural analogs when supporting an obviousness rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using such sources, examiners should make clear factual findings and reasoning connecting the evidence to the conclusion that a skilled artisan would have been motivated to combine or modify references with a reasonable expectation of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written Description Requirement (§ 112(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must find adequate support within the specification demonstrating that the inventor possessed the full scope of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the specification describes the claimed invention in sufficient detail to show possession of the claimed subject matter across its full scope. Mere recitation of claim language without adequate descriptive support can fail this requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement Requirement (§ 112(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must enable persons skilled in the art to 'make and use' the invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the disclosure provides sufficient teaching to allow skilled artisans to practice the claimed invention across the full scope without undue experimentation. Consider the predictability of the art and the amount of experimentation required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity / Definiteness Requirement (§ 112(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention; claim language that lacks ordinary meaning or clarity is indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject claims when terms are ambiguous, lack antecedent basis, or otherwise fail to inform a skilled artisan of the scope with reasonable certainty. Applicants may respond by narrowing claim scope, adding antecedent basis, or supplying structural limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common Indefiniteness Issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative problems include functional limitations without structure, relative terminology lacking clarity, antecedent basis failures, and aggregated limitations without meaningful relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When examining for indefiniteness, look for unsupported functional language, undefined relative terms (e.g., 'substantially', 'about' without context), missing antecedent references, and claim element aggregations that do not indicate how elements interact. Require amendments or clarifying disclosure as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: §101 Eligibility — Examiner Rejection Standard and Applicant Responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Ground: §101 Eligibility. Burden: Prima facie rejection using claim analysis. Applicant Response: Demonstrate integration into practical application or add 'significantly more' limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should identify why a claim is directed to a judicial exception and provide analysis; applicants can respond by amending claims to include technological improvements, demonstrating practical application, or arguing the claims already include 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: §102 Anticipation — Examiner Rejection Standard and Applicant Responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Ground: §102 Anticipation. Burden: Single reference disclosure or admission. Applicant Response: Antedate reference, show the reference is non-enabling, or claim narrow distinctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must point to the single reference elements that anticipate every claim limitation. Applicants may submit affidavits/declarations to antedate or argue non-enablement of the reference, or amend claims to distinguish the reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: §103 Obviousness — Examiner Rejection Standard and Applicant Responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Ground: §103 Obviousness. Burden: Motivation + reasonable expectation of success. Applicant Response: Present secondary considerations, unpredictability, or argue narrow claim scope to overcome obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should articulate the reasoning and evidence supporting a motivation to combine and expectation of success. Applicants can rebut with objective indicia of non-obviousness (e.g., unexpected results) or demonstrate that the combination would have been unpredictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: §112 Definiteness — Examiner Rejection Standard and Applicant Responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Ground: §112 Definiteness. Burden: Terms lack ordinary meaning. Applicant Response: Narrow scope, add antecedent basis, or provide structural limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When issuing a §112 rejection, identify the specific terms or claim language that are indefinite and explain why. Applicants should amend claims or provide explanations/definitions in the specification to clarify claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulating Rejections — Identification and Reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners must clearly identify which limitation(s) trigger a rejection and provide reasoning connecting evidence to conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejections should map claim limitations to prior art or explain how claim language implicates a judicial exception. Provide factual findings and step-by-step reasoning so applicants can understand and respond effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined Analysis (§ 2106.06)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility may be self-evident for clearly patentable subject matter; detailed analysis may be waived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For claims that are clearly directed to patent-eligible subject matter, examiners can apply a streamlined analysis and need not perform the full stepwise eligibility framework. Document when and why streamlined analysis is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavits/Declarations (§ 2155) to Overcome Prior Art Rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may overcome prior art rejections by submitting affidavits/declarations showing inventor-originated disclosures or that references lack enablement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applicants provide evidence (e.g., affidavits) that a reference is not prior art or is non-enabling, examiners must evaluate the sufficiency and probative value of the evidence in the context of the rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Interpretation Standard — Broadest Reasonable Interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: During prosecution, claim terms are given their broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret claim language with plain meaning consistent with the specification as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art. Apply broadest reasonable interpretation when construing claim terms for examination purposes.
